evidence: books/nntp-auth.lisp:1494-1499: the only 502 arm is `((fn-auth-session-tlsp as) (fn-post-make-result as (fn-auth-single as (fn-proto-text "STARTTLS" :active)) nil))`. The session subject is never tested, and the 382 arm resets the session with `(fn-auth-make-session ... nil nil nil t ...)`. books/nntp-auth.lisp:875-879: `(defun fn-auth-starttls-lines (acfg tlsp) (if (and (fn-auth-config-tls-availablep acfg) (not tlsp)) (list (fn-nntp-string-octets "STARTTLS")) nil))` takes no subject. RFC 4642 section 2.1 says STARTTLS 'MUST NOT be advertised ... after successful authentication', and section 2.2.1 note [1] says that 'if authentication has occurred, STARTTLS is not a valid command' (502).
fix: In fn-auth-starttls, add an arm before the 382 branch: `((fn-auth-session-subject as) ... (fn-proto-text "STARTTLS" :active))`, which gives 502. Pass the subject to fn-auth-starttls-lines (from fn-auth-access-capability-lines) and omit STARTTLS when it is set. Add the reachable witness and the hypothesis-removal witness.
reviewer: fn-auth-starttls (books/nntp-auth.lisp:1482-1520) has one 502 arm, for tlsp (:1496-1498), and never tests fn-auth-session-subject. fn-auth-starttls-lines (:875-879) takes no subject, so STARTTLS is still advertised after a successful AUTHINFO. Plaintext AUTHINFO USER/PASS succeeds on any listener that is not protected-only (the 483 arm at :1330-1334 is protected-only). The sequence AUTHINFO 281, then STARTTLS, therefore gets 382, which breaks RFC 4642 2.1/2.2.1 (502 is required). The 382 arm clears the subject and the principal peer. Severity is low: it is a protocol conformance bug, and an attacker able to inject STARTTLS into a plaintext session already controls that session.
scenario: On a listener without protected-only, a client authenticates with AUTHINFO USER/PASS (281), and CAPABILITIES still lists STARTTLS. The client issues STARTTLS and gets 382 instead of 502. The session subject and pending login are cleared, and any principal-bound peer role is dropped (fn-auth-clear-principal-peer). After the handshake the client is unauthenticated with no error reported, and on a requires-auth node its next GROUP gets 480. An active attacker who can inject 'STARTTLS' can force the downgrade or reset, and the code the RFC prescribes for refusing is never produced.
title: STARTTLS after successful authentication is answered 382 (and still advertised) instead of 502, silently dropping the authenticated identity
